title: Regex Basics
description: Match patterns in text with re — find, extract, and replace using a small set of metacharacters that cover most real-world cases.
objectives: Use `re.search`, `re.findall`, and `re.sub` to find and rewrite text
Read and write the small set of metacharacters that cover 90% of real cases
Recognize when a regex is the wrong tool — and reach for `str` methods or a parser instead

completionRules.expected:
all numbers: ['404', '500', '200']
first error code: 404
redacted: Error ###: not found. Then later, error ### happened. Final code ###.

checks.name: Use re.findall
checks.feedback: Call re.findall inside analyze_text() to derive the numbers.

checks.name: Use re.search
checks.feedback: Call re.search inside analyze_text() to derive the first error code.

checks.name: Use re.sub
checks.feedback: Call re.sub inside analyze_text() to derive the redacted text.

recap: A regex is a pattern that describes a *shape* of text. `re.search` finds the first match (or `None`); `re.findall` returns every match as a list; `re.sub(pattern, replacement, text)` rewrites every match. The most useful metacharacters are `\d` (digit), `\w` (word char), `\s` (whitespace), `+` (one or more), `*` (zero or more), `?` (optional), `[abc]` (one of), and `()` (capture group). Reach for a regex when you're matching a *shape*; reach for `str.split` / `str.startswith` / a real parser when you're not.
practicePrompts: Take a regex you wrote here and feed it tricky input — empty string, very long string, edge cases at the start/end. Does it still do what you expected?
When is a regex the *wrong* answer? (Hint: parsing HTML, parsing a programming language, anything with nested structure.)

practiceExercises.title: Find every email
practiceExercises.prompt:
Write `find_emails(text)` that returns a list of every simple email address in `text`, in the order they appear. For this exercise, an email is `<word>@<word>.<word>` — letters, digits, and underscores only. Use `re.findall`.

For example, `find_emails("contact alice@example.com or bob@test.org")` returns `["alice@example.com", "bob@test.org"]`.

(In real code you'd use a more permissive pattern — RFC-compliant email regexes are notoriously gnarly. This is fine for the lesson.)
practiceExercises.goal: Use re.findall with a multi-part pattern to extract every match.

    pass
hints: `re.findall(pattern, text)` returns a list of every non-overlapping match. The pattern just needs to describe the *shape* of an email.

Shape:
```python
import re
re.findall(r"\w+@\w+\.\w+", text)
```
`\w+` is one or more word chars; `\.` is a literal dot (the backslash is needed because `.` alone matches any character). Wrap the whole pattern in `r"..."` (raw string) so backslashes don't need to be doubled.

The same shape for a different target — phone numbers like 555-1234:
```python
re.findall(r"\d{3}-\d{4}", text)
```
`\d{3}` is exactly three digits.

practiceExercises.title: First phone number
practiceExercises.prompt:
Write `first_phone(text)` that returns the first phone number in `text` formatted like `555-1234` (three digits, hyphen, four digits). If there's no match, return `None`. Use `re.search`.

For example, `first_phone("call 555-1234 or 999-7777")` returns `"555-1234"`. `first_phone("no number here")` returns `None`.

hints: `re.search` returns either a *match object* (truthy) or `None` (falsy). The match object has a `.group()` method that gives you the matched string back.

The same pattern with a *capture group*, returning just the digits without the prefix:
```python
m = re.search(r"HTTP (\d{3})", text)
if m:
    return m.group(1)
```
With parentheses around `\d{3}`, `m.group(1)` returns *just the digits*, not the surrounding `HTTP `.

practiceExercises.title: Redact every email
practiceExercises.prompt:
Write `redact_emails(text)` that returns `text` with every email address replaced by the literal string `"[email]"`. Use the same simple email pattern as the first exercise: `\w+@\w+\.\w+`. Use `re.sub`.

For example, `redact_emails("alice@x.com and bob@y.org")` returns `"[email] and [email]"`. If there are no emails, return `text` unchanged.
practiceExercises.goal: Use re.sub to rewrite every match in a string.

hints: `re.sub(pattern, replacement, text)` walks every match in `text` and replaces it with `replacement`, returning the new string. The original is untouched.

Shape:
```python
import re
re.sub(r"\w+@\w+\.\w+", "[email]", text)
```
The replacement string is plain text — no escaping needed for the brackets.

The same pattern collapsing all whitespace to a single space:
```python
re.sub(r"\s+", " ", text)
```
`\s+` matches one or more whitespace characters.
